newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Copper squeeze eases, for now.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Copper squeeze eases, for now.

text.p: Trading in copper became erratic on Monday when an extreme technical squeeze on nearby supplies unravelled viciously on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
Fundamentals of supply and demand continue to suggest tight prospects but, at least on Monday, and despite the squeeze by at least one big player, enough metal was made available to the market.

The premium of cash over three months copper, which stood at $210 per tonne at one stage, contracted to $93 by the end of afternoon trading. Three months copper also ended the session down $27 at $2,356 per tonne.
Traders and analysts were nonplussed by Monday's action.
"This market is totally confused...but the short-term fundamentals are supportive, which is playing into the hands of the longs,' said Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME broker Billiton Metals Ltd.

The squeeze, which has been massaged by strong investment players, is taking place against a background of supply disputes in Chile, the largest producer, falling global stocks, and a temporary closure of a big smelter in the United States.
Traders said that this has coincided with major short positions falling due.
"There is a big short that keeps on getting rolled forward. It happened at the end of October, January, end-April, and is now being pushed to the end of July," one said.
Nearby premiums could now contract further, although many remain wary of further tightness.
"As long as the stocks are low and still falling there is still the potential for further squeezes," MacMillan said.

Elsewhere in commodity markets, benchmark Chicago wheat prices were somewhat easier around $4.25 per bushel, after a 1997 high above $4.50 a week ago to which they were driven by fears of crop damage from floods and a freeze in North America and drought in Europe.

But although short-term concerns have somewhat abated, some traders and analysts saw prospects of a new spike in prices because of weather problems and low world grain stocks. Wheat hit $7.50 a year ago.
One of the worst winter droughts in the last 150 years has destroyed an estimated 50 to 70 percent of Portugal's winter cereal crops, an Agriculture Ministry official said on Monday.
Deputy Secretary of State for Agriculture Carlos Cunha said that rain last week in the cereal-producing Alentejo region might save pasture but not winter cereal crops, predominantly wheat.
"Even if it rains from now until the end of May it won't save winter crops. It's too late," Cunha told Reuters.

Rain fell at the weekend in dry areas of England and France but experts said more was needed. The European Union last week put a tax on wheat exports to curb sales abroad and keep a lid on internal prices.

Low world wheat stocks and uncertain weather have created the same set of forces which this time last year sent prices spiralling upward, according to Mark Martin, managing director of consultancy Agracom Risk Management in Australia.
"We now have prices of $4.50 with the potential for ending stocks lower than 100 million tonnes. It's highly conceivable we could see a similar rally to... last year," he said.
Coffee prices have retreated after news that truck drivers in Colombia, the second biggest grower, agreed to end a six-day strike that had threatened supply.
London July futures for robusta beans ended down $28 at $1,600 per tonne after speculative buyers retreated and origin countries resumed selling. Cocoa also eased.
Gold was also edging down for want of speculative interest. Oil prices were little changed.
